en.title: Guidance and Counselling: the whole course
en.short: What guidance and counselling covers, how degrees are organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Guidance and counselling is the study and practice of helping people understand themselves, make decisions and cope with difficulties. Guidance is the wider service. It gives information and direction, for example about subjects, careers or school rules. Counselling is a more personal helping relationship. A trained counsellor listens carefully, helps the client explore feelings and choices, and supports change without taking over the client’s decisions. The field draws on psychology, education, human development, assessment and ethics. It is used in schools, colleges, hospitals, workplaces, community agencies and private practice. Counsellors do not usually prescribe medicine. In many places, counselling is distinct from clinical psychology and psychiatry, though they work together. The course trains both understanding and controlled helping skills.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text: Programmes differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook for length, award and requirements. In Nigerian universities, guidance and counselling is commonly offered as a Bachelor of Education (BEd) degree, often over four years, with courses in education and counselling. Postgraduate awards include MEd and PhD. The Counselling Association of Nigeria (CASSON) is a professional association. In the United Kingdom, many counsellors train through diplomas or postgraduate courses rather than a single standard undergraduate degree, and bodies such as the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy (BACP) maintain accreditation registers. In the United States, professional counselling is commonly entered through a master’s degree, and licensure is set by each state. Do not assume that one country’s route applies in another.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage gives the foundation. You begin with the concepts, goals and scope of guidance and counselling, then the history of the field. You study human growth and development, personality and individual differences, and the communication skills that build a helping relationship. Basic microskills come next: attending, listening, questioning, reflecting and summarising. You then meet the main counselling theories, ethical principles, research and measurement, and self-awareness for professional development.

The core stage applies this foundation. It covers psychodynamic and Adlerian counselling; person-centred and existential counselling; cognitive-behavioural and rational emotive counselling; and solution-focused and narrative counselling. You then study career guidance, educational guidance and school counselling, personal and social counselling, group counselling, family and couple counselling, and counselling children and adolescents. Assessment and psychometrics, crisis intervention and grief counselling, and substance use and addiction counselling follow. Multicultural and diversity counselling runs alongside professional practice, law and ethics. The practicum and case management turn theory into supervised practice, and research methods and programme evaluation show how to judge a service.

At master’s level, the work becomes more advanced. You study counselling theory and integration, advanced research methods and a dissertation, and supervision and training. The aim is to think critically, conduct research and support other counsellors.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Read each theory actively. For every approach, learn the main idea, the key terms, the view of the person, the role of the counsellor and one criticism. Compare theories instead of memorising lists. Practise skills in role-play and record sessions where this is allowed. Ask for feedback on listening, questioning and reflection. Keep a reflective journal, but protect confidentiality by using initials or disguised details.

Link each topic to a setting: school, clinic, workplace or community service. Learn the ethical code and the law that apply where you plan to work, and check current official sources because rules change. Use case notes and supervision to connect theory with practice. For research, read a study’s method before accepting its conclusion.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text:
One common mistake is to confuse guidance with counselling. Giving information is not the same as helping a person explore feelings. Another is to give advice too quickly, or to use one theory as if it fitted every client. Students also forget culture, family and social context, or treat a textbook example as universal.

Ethical mistakes are serious. These include breaking confidentiality without good reason, seeing clients beyond your competence, and using tests without training. Poor case notes and failure to seek supervision are common. In research, students sometimes claim that a small sample proves a general rule, or confuse correlation with cause. Learn the limits of your evidence.

keyPoints: Guidance is the wider information and support service; counselling is a personal helping relationship.
Counselling courses combine human development, skills, theories, ethics, assessment, practice and research.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Learn each theory with its main claim, key terms and limits, and compare theories rather than memorising lists.
Practise listening and responding skills through role-play, feedback and supervised cases.
Confidentiality, competence and supervision are central ethical duties in counselling.

en.title: Guidance and Counselling: Concepts, Goals and Scope
en.short: Definitions, goals, settings, client groups, misconceptions and scope of guidance and counselling.

sections.heading: Defining the terms
sections.text: Guidance is organised help that gives people information and support so they can make decisions about education, work or life. It is often educational, preventive and can be given in groups. Counselling is a confidential, structured helping relationship in which a trained counsellor helps a person explore feelings, thoughts and choices and make their own decisions. Guidance is broader and more informational; counselling is more personal and relational. Both aim at development, not dependence.

sections.heading: Counselling and its neighbours
sections.text: Counselling differs from psychotherapy mainly in depth, duration and focus. Psychotherapy is usually longer and treats deeper or clinical psychological problems; counselling is often shorter and developmental. The two overlap, and laws on who may practise vary by country, so check local rules. Counselling also differs from giving advice. Advice tells a person what to do. Counselling explores options, clarifies values and helps the person decide. A counsellor may share information, but does not take over the choice.

sections.heading: Goals, settings and clients
sections.text: Common goals are self-understanding, better decision-making, coping skills, personal growth and change. Settings include schools, colleges, universities, clinics, workplaces, community agencies and online services. Clients include children, adolescents, adults, couples, families and groups. A student may seek guidance about course requirements, or counselling about anxiety and study stress. Counselling is not only for serious mental illness, and seeking help is not a sign of weakness.

sections.heading: Misconceptions and scope
sections.text: Misconceptions include: counselling is just advice; the counsellor solves the problem; it is only for “mad” people; and confidentiality is always absolute. Confidentiality has legal and safety limits, explained in ethics. The field’s scope includes educational, career and personal-social counselling, group and family work, crisis support, assessment, ethics, supervision and research. A first-year student, Amina, cannot choose between two courses. Guidance gives her facts about requirements. Counselling helps her explore fear of failure and decide for herself.

keyPoints: Guidance is broader and more informational than counselling, which is a confidential helping relationship.
Counselling is usually shorter and more developmental than psychotherapy, though they overlap.
Counselling is not advice-giving; it helps clients explore options and make their own decisions.
Goals include self-understanding, decision-making, coping and personal growth.
Counselling serves many settings and client groups, not only people with serious mental illness.
Confidentiality is important but has legal and safety limits.

en.title: History and Development of Guidance and Counselling
en.short: Vocational guidance and mental health movements grew into school and community counselling in Africa and Nigeria.

sections.heading: Early roots
sections.text:
Guidance and counselling grew from two streams. Vocational guidance helped people choose work as industrial cities expanded in Europe and North America in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Frank Parsons, an American reformer, is often linked with its early practice. The mental health movement pressed for humane care and prevention, not only treatment. These streams met in schools, clinics and community agencies.

Guidance means organised help with choices about education, work and personal life. Counselling is a professional helping relationship. The history shows a shift from job advice towards broader support.

sections.heading: Schools and community
sections.text:
School guidance services developed in the early twentieth century, especially in the United States, and later spread elsewhere. They added educational guidance, career information, testing and personal support. After the Second World War many countries expanded school counselling, but pace and model differed. Some employed full-time counsellors; others used teacher-counsellors.

Community counselling grew through mental health centres, youth services, family agencies and non-governmental organisations. It reached people outside schools. In many low-income settings, services rely on trained volunteers and referral networks.

sections.heading: Africa and Nigeria
sections.text:
Guidance and counselling in Africa has diverse roots. Before formal services, elders, religious leaders, teachers and families gave advice. Formal school guidance expanded with education systems, urbanisation and youth employment concerns. Universities began training counsellors, and ministries of education introduced guidance units. Patterns vary widely by country.

In Nigeria, guidance and counselling grew mainly through schools and teacher training from the mid-twentieth century, then universities. The Counselling Association of Nigeria (CASSON) is a major professional association. It promotes training, ethics and conferences. Government agencies and state school systems also shape practice.

sections.heading: Professional bodies
sections.text: Professional bodies set codes of ethics, training standards, conferences and journals. In some countries government boards license counsellors; in others associations lead. Case: Amina, a first-year student in Kano, sees a school counsellor about course choice. The counsellor uses career information and refers her for financial advice. This shows school and community services working together.

keyPoints: Guidance and counselling grew from vocational guidance and mental health movements.
Vocational guidance helped people choose work; mental health movements sought humane care and prevention.
School guidance added educational, career and personal support, while community services reached people outside schools.
African histories are diverse; formal services built on existing family, religious and community support.
In Nigeria, school and teacher training played a major role, and CASSON is a major professional association.
Professional bodies set ethics and training standards, but licensing arrangements differ by country.

en.title: Human Growth and Development for Counsellors
en.short: Physical, cognitive, social, emotional and moral development and their use in counselling.

sections.heading: What development means
sections.text: Development is the pattern of change in physical, cognitive, social, emotional and moral functioning from conception to death. Physical development covers body growth, motor skills, puberty and ageing. Cognitive development covers thinking, memory and reasoning. Social development is how relationships and roles change. Emotional development is recognising and regulating feelings. Moral development is reasoning about right and wrong. These strands interact; a sick child may regress socially, and a teenager’s puberty affects self-image.

sections.heading: Stages and tasks
sections.text: Stage theories describe common sequences, not fixed timetables. Piaget proposed four cognitive stages: sensorimotor (about 0-2), preoperational (2-7), concrete operational (7-11) and formal operational (from about 11). Erikson described psychosocial tasks: trust in infancy, autonomy and initiative in early childhood, industry at school age, identity in adolescence, intimacy in young adulthood, generativity in middle age and integrity in later life. Kohlberg described moral reasoning as preconventional (right and wrong judged by punishment and reward), conventional (judged by rules and others’ approval) and postconventional (judged by personal principles); not everyone reaches the later levels, and cultural critics question his scale. Havighurst’s developmental tasks are the skills society expects at each period, such as forming friendships, choosing work and adjusting to ageing.

sections.heading: Development in counselling
sections.text: These ideas guide assessment. A 7-year-old usually reasons concretely, so a counsellor uses simple words, drawing or play. An adolescent is often working on identity and autonomy, so counselling respects privacy and explores values without lecturing. An adult may bring work, marriage or parenting concerns; an older adult may bring loss, illness or retirement. The counsellor matches the approach to the person’s developmental level, not only age. Example: Amina, 15, in Kaduna, is torn between family expectations and peer pressure. The counsellor listens, clarifies her values, and plans small steps with her, involving parents only with her agreement and within safeguarding rules.

keyPoints: Development has physical, cognitive, social, emotional and moral strands that interact.
Piaget, Erikson, Kohlberg and Havighurst describe common sequences and tasks, not fixed timetables.
Developmental stage shapes the concerns clients bring and the language and methods a counsellor uses.
Match counselling to developmental level, not age alone, and allow for individual and cultural variation.
Use concrete methods with young children and respect autonomy and confidentiality with adolescents, within safeguarding rules.
Moral reasoning develops through levels, but not everyone reaches the highest and cultural context matters.

en.title: Personality and Individual Differences in Counselling
en.short: Major personality perspectives and how temperament, ability, interests and values shape counselling.

sections.heading: Perspectives on personality
sections.text: Personality is a person’s fairly stable pattern of thinking, feeling and behaving. Trait theory describes broad dimensions that differ between people; the Big Five model names openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Psychodynamic theory looks at unconscious conflict and early relationships. Humanistic theory stresses growth, self-concept and conditions of worth. Social-cognitive theory focuses on learning, expectations, self-efficacy (belief in one’s ability to act) and the situation. Biological theory links personality to heredity, temperament and brain or body processes. Each view explains some behaviour; none is complete.

sections.heading: Temperament, ability, interests, values
sections.text: Temperament is early-emerging emotional reactivity and self-regulation, partly biological. Ability is what a person can do or learn, such as reasoning or aptitude. Interests are preferences for activities; values are guiding beliefs about what matters. These differ from personality but overlap with it. A student may have strong interest in medicine but weaker science grades, or high ability but different values. Counsellors explore all four rather than assuming one predicts success.

sections.heading: Counselling without labels
sections.text: Individual differences shape how a client communicates, copes and chooses goals. A counsellor may adapt pace, structure or career exploration, but should not use a type or score as a fixed label. Labels can lower expectations and ignore culture, health, poverty and opportunity. Use results as hypotheses, check them with the client, and keep person-first language. Personality tests can support discussion only when reliable, valid and used within the counsellor’s training and local ethical rules. Case: Amina and Tunde both fail a test. Amina is anxious and seeks reassurance; Tunde is calm and wants practical planning. The counsellor listens to each, avoids calling one “weak”, and agrees different next steps.

keyPoints: Personality is a fairly stable pattern of thinking, feeling and behaving.
Trait, psychodynamic, humanistic, social-cognitive and biological views each explain part of personality.
Temperament is early-emerging reactivity and self-regulation; ability, interests and values are related but distinct.
Individual differences should guide communication and goals, not justify fixed labels.
Use test results as hypotheses, check them with the client, and consider culture and context.
Person-first language and client collaboration reduce harm from labelling.

en.title: Communication and the Helping Relationship
en.short: Core conditions, structure, confidentiality and boundaries in counselling communication.

sections.heading: A purposeful relationship
sections.text: Counselling is a planned, professional relationship with an agreed purpose, time and place. Unlike ordinary conversation, it is client-led: the counsellor listens and helps the client explore, rather than exchanging news or giving quick advice. The relationship usually moves through a beginning (welcome, contract, confidentiality), a middle (exploring concerns and goals), and an ending (review, plan, closure). A contract is the agreement about time, fees if any, contact between sessions and limits.

sections.heading: Core conditions
sections.text: Carl Rogers described three core conditions: empathy, unconditional positive regard and congruence. Empathy means understanding the client’s feelings and meaning and showing that understanding. Unconditional positive regard is warmth and respect without judging the person’s worth. Congruence, or genuineness, means the counsellor is real and consistent, not hiding behind a role. Respect accepts the client as capable. Warmth is shown by tone, welcome and steady attention. These conditions are ways of being, not just techniques.

sections.heading: Confidentiality and boundaries
sections.text: Confidentiality means not sharing what a client says without consent. It has limits: risk of serious harm, legal requirements and supervision. Tell clients these limits at the start. Boundaries are clear rules about time, place, fees, self-disclosure, gifts and contact outside sessions. They protect both people and keep the relationship focused. Example: a first-year student tells a counsellor he is failing and feels ashamed. The counsellor keeps the session private, agrees goals, and does not promise secrecy if there is serious risk.

sections.heading: Purposeful communication
sections.text: In counselling, communication is purposeful. The counsellor uses questions, reflections and summaries to help the client think and checks understanding before moving on. Ordinary conversation often shifts to the helper’s own stories; counselling keeps the focus on the client. Self-disclosure is used only when it serves the client. The counsellor also watches tone, body language and silence. These help the client feel heard and safe enough to talk.

keyPoints: The helping relationship is planned, client-led and limited in time, place and purpose.
The core conditions are empathy, unconditional positive regard and congruence or genuineness.
Empathy is understanding and communicating the client’s feelings and meaning.
Confidentiality protects what the client shares but has limits such as serious risk and legal requirements.
Boundaries cover time, fees, contact, self-disclosure and gifts, and protect both people.
Counselling communication is purposeful and keeps focus on the client, unlike ordinary conversation.

en.title: Basic Counselling Microskills
en.short: Attending, listening, paraphrasing, summarising, reflecting feelings, questioning, silence, immediacy and confrontation.

sections.heading: Attending and active listening
sections.text: Counselling microskills are the small, learnable skills a counsellor uses in every session. Attending behaviour is how a counsellor shows physical availability: face the client squarely, open posture, lean slightly forward, keep relaxed eye contact, and stay relaxed (often taught as SOLER). Active listening means hearing content and feeling, then showing you heard. In a case, Chidi says he failed a test and feels ashamed. The counsellor nods, keeps eye contact and says, 'You failed and you feel ashamed.' That is a reflection, not a question. Practice: in pairs, one speaks for two minutes while the other only attends and reflects; swap. Common mistake: looking away, writing too much, or planning your reply instead of listening.

sections.heading: Paraphrasing, summarising, reflecting feelings
sections.text: A paraphrase restates the client’s main content in your own words: 'So the exam was harder than you expected.' A summary gathers several points, often at the end of a session. Reflecting feelings names the emotion you hear: 'You sound disappointed.' Use feeling words carefully and check: 'Is that right?' Practice: after a five-minute story, give one paraphrase and one feeling reflection. Common mistakes: parroting the client’s exact words, adding your own interpretation, or naming a feeling the client did not show.

sections.heading: Questions, silence, immediacy, confrontation
sections.text: Open questions ('What happened next?') invite detail; closed questions ('Did you tell your teacher?') give yes or no and are useful for facts. Silence gives space to think and feel; do not fill every pause. Immediacy talks about what is happening between you now: 'I notice you look away when we discuss your father.' Confrontation, in counselling, is a gentle pointing out of a mismatch between words and behaviour, not an attack: 'You say you want to study, but you miss every session.' Practice: record a role-play and count open questions, closed questions and silences. Common mistakes: asking many questions in a row, using silence to punish, or confronting before trust is built.

keyPoints: Attending behaviour shows physical availability through posture, eye contact and relaxed presence.
Active listening means hearing both content and feeling and showing that you heard.
A paraphrase restates content; a summary gathers several points; a feeling reflection names emotion.
Open questions invite detail, closed questions give facts, and silence allows thinking.
Immediacy addresses what is happening between counsellor and client in the moment.
Confrontation gently points out a mismatch, and it needs trust and care.

en.title: Introduction to Counselling Theories
en.short: Why counsellors use theory, the five main families, and how formulation, goals and techniques fit together.

sections.heading: Why counsellors use theory
sections.text:
A theory is an organised set of ideas that explains how people change and guides what a counsellor does. Without one, a session becomes guesswork. A theory helps the counsellor decide what to notice, how to understand a problem, and which methods to try. It also gives a shared language for supervision and research, and a way to check whether the work is helping.

No single theory fits every person. Most training introduces several, then later teaches integration, which means combining ideas from more than one approach in a planned way.

sections.heading: The main families
sections.text:
Psychodynamic theories, from Freud, hold that early relationships and unconscious feelings shape present behaviour; the counsellor listens for patterns and hidden meaning. Humanistic theories, such as person-centred counselling (Rogers), trust the person’s own capacity to grow and stress empathy, warmth and genuineness. Cognitive-behavioural theories say distress comes from learned and unhelpful thoughts and actions, so they work on changing both.

Systemic theories see the person inside a family or network and treat the relationships, not only the individual. Postmodern theories include narrative approaches, which treat problems as stories people can re-author, and solution-focused approaches, which look at what is already working.

sections.heading: Formulation, goals, techniques
sections.text:
A formulation is the counsellor’s working explanation of why this person has this problem now: the presenting concern, its history, what keeps it going, and the person’s strengths. It links theory to action. Goals are agreed outcomes, set with the client, and should be specific enough to review. Techniques are the concrete methods a theory suggests, such as free association, reflective listening, thought records or circular questioning.

Theories differ in what they emphasise: insight, behaviour or relationships.

sections.heading: A short case
sections.text: Consider Amina, 19, who panics before exams. A cognitive-behavioural counsellor would map her thoughts ("I will fail"), plan a thought record and a study routine. A person-centred counsellor would first offer space and acceptance. Both are defensible; the choice depends on the client, the setting and the counsellor’s training.

keyPoints: A theory explains how people change and guides what the counsellor notices, aims at and does.
The five main families are psychodynamic, humanistic, cognitive-behavioural, systemic and postmodern.
A formulation links theory to action by explaining why this person has this problem now.
Goals are agreed with the client and should be specific enough to review.
Techniques such as thought records or reflective listening belong to particular theories, not to counselling in general.
No single theory suits every client, so training usually teaches several and later teaches integration.

en.title: Ethical Principles in Guidance and Counselling
en.short: The six ethical principles, consent, confidentiality, competence, boundaries, referral and records.

sections.heading: Six principles
sections.text: Autonomy means respecting the client’s right to make informed choices. Beneficence means working for the client’s good. Non-maleficence means avoiding harm. Justice means fair treatment, fair access to help and non-discrimination. Fidelity means keeping promises, being reliable and building trust. Veracity means being honest, including about the limits of one’s competence. These principles can conflict. A client may choose a course that seems unwise, and the counsellor must balance respect for that choice with the duty to prevent harm.

sections.heading: Consent and confidentiality
sections.text: Informed consent means the client agrees after understanding the purpose, methods, possible risks and benefits, alternatives, and the right to withdraw. Consent must be voluntary and the client must have capacity. Confidentiality means keeping what the client says private. Its limits must be explained at the start: risk of serious harm to the client or others, child protection concerns, court orders, and supervision or consultation. A concrete case: a client discloses that a child is being abused. The counsellor explains the limit, protects the child under local law, and shares only what is necessary.

sections.heading: Competence and boundaries
sections.text: Competence means having the training, skills and experience for the work, and knowing when to refer. Referral means passing the client to a suitable professional, with consent where possible. Boundaries are clear professional limits. They protect the client and counsellor, and they rule out exploitation, secret personal relationships and dual roles that impair judgement. Record keeping should be factual, timely, secure and kept only as long as local rules require. Clients may have a right to see their records under local law. Codes differ by country and professional body, so check the current code that governs your setting.

keyPoints: Autonomy respects the client’s right to choose; beneficence seeks good and non-maleficence avoids harm.
Justice means fairness and non-discrimination; fidelity means trustworthiness; veracity means honesty.
Informed consent must be voluntary and based on full information.
Confidentiality has limits that must be explained early.
Counsellors work within competence, keep clear boundaries and refer when needed.
Keep factual, secure records and follow the current code for your country and professional body.

en.title: Introduction to Research and Measurement in Counselling
en.short: Covers why evidence matters, key research terms, reliability, validity, bias and simple statistics.

sections.heading: Why evidence matters
sections.text: Counsellors need evidence because helping is not harmless. A method that feels right may not work, and may cause harm. Evidence from research helps counsellors choose approaches, explain decisions, and remain accountable. It does not replace clinical judgement or the client’s view; it informs them. Personal opinion comes from one person’s experience. Research evidence comes from planned study, with methods open to checking.

sections.heading: Key research terms
sections.text: A variable is any characteristic that can differ, such as age, anxiety score or number of sessions. The population is everyone the question concerns. A sample is the smaller group actually studied. Reliability means consistency: the same measure gives similar results on repeated use. Validity means the measure assesses what it claims to assess. Bias is a systematic error that pushes results in one direction, for example asking only clients who stayed in therapy.

sections.heading: Measuring and summarising
sections.text: Descriptive statistics summarise a sample. The mean is the total divided by the number of scores. The median is the middle score when values are ordered. The mode is the most frequent score. The range is the highest score minus the lowest. Suppose five clients rate a service 4, 5, 3, 4 and 4. Mean = 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Ordered: 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, so median = 4. Mode = 4. Range = 5 − 3 = 2.

sections.heading: Evidence or opinion
sections.text: An opinion may be useful, but it is not evidence unless tested. A single case can suggest a question; a sample study can answer it. Read claims by asking: what was measured, who was sampled, how reliable and valid were the measures, and what bias could remain?

keyPoints: Counsellors need research evidence to choose safe, effective methods and to be accountable.
A variable is a characteristic that can differ; a population is the whole group of interest and a sample is the part studied.
Reliability is consistency; validity is whether a measure assesses what it claims; bias is systematic error.
Mean = sum of scores ÷ number of scores; median = middle ordered score; mode = most frequent score; range = highest − lowest.
Research evidence comes from planned, checkable study; personal opinion comes from individual experience and is not proof.
In the example 4, 5, 3, 4, 4, the mean is 4, the median is 4, the mode is 4 and the range is 2.

en.title: Self-Awareness and Professional Development
en.short: Reflective practice, values, bias, transference, supervision and self-care for counsellors.

sections.heading: Self-awareness in practice
sections.text: Self-awareness means noticing your own feelings, beliefs, history and limits. The counsellor is part of the helping relationship. Family patterns, culture, past losses and hopes shape what you notice, avoid and how you respond. A counsellor never allowed to express anger may change the subject when a client is angry. Reflective practice is thinking carefully about these reactions, using a journal, feedback and supervision. The aim is not to have no history, but to stop your history deciding for the client.

sections.heading: Values and bias
sections.text: Values clarification is naming what you believe about right and wrong, family, work, religion and sex, and asking how those beliefs affect counselling. Personal biases are strong preferences or prejudices that can distort judgement. Some are explicit; others are implicit, meaning outside immediate awareness. A counsellor who believes a woman should stay in marriage may struggle to hear a client’s wish to leave. Reflection helps but does not remove bias. Ask for feedback and check assumptions in supervision.

sections.heading: Transference and countertransference
sections.text: Transference is when a client reacts to the counsellor as if the counsellor were someone from the client’s past, such as a critical parent. Countertransference is the counsellor’s emotional reaction to the client, which may come from the counsellor’s own history. For example, Ngozi, a trainee in Lagos, feels unusually protective of Tunde, whose father left home. She offers extra sessions and feels hurt when he cancels. In supervision she sees that her own father’s absence shapes her response. She returns to agreed boundaries and explores Tunde’s feelings without acting on hers.

sections.heading: Supervision and self-care
sections.text: Supervision is regular, structured consultation with an experienced counsellor about your work. It is not a sign of failure. It helps you notice blind spots, plan safely and separate your needs from the client’s. Self-care means maintaining your health through sleep, exercise, rest, support and limits on workload. It protects clients too, because a tired counsellor cannot listen well. Use supervision and seek personal therapy if issues keep interfering.

keyPoints: Self-awareness helps counsellors notice how their own history, culture and feelings shape their work.
Reflective practice uses journaling, feedback and supervision to examine reactions and assumptions.
Values clarification names personal beliefs, while bias is a preference or prejudice that can distort judgement.
Transference is the client’s reaction to the counsellor as if from a past relationship; countertransference is the counsellor’s reaction to the client.
Supervision is structured consultation about your work, not a sign of failure.
Self-care protects both counsellor and client, and personal therapy is indicated when personal issues interfere.

en.title: Psychodynamic and Adlerian Counselling
en.short: Freudian and Adlerian concepts, goals, techniques, a case formulation and evidence limits.

sections.heading: Freudian ideas
sections.text: Freud held that much mental life is unconscious: wishes, memories and conflicts outside awareness still shape behaviour. Defence mechanisms are unconscious strategies that reduce anxiety, such as repression (pushing a thought away), projection (seeing one’s own feeling in another) and rationalisation (giving a plausible but untrue reason). Transference occurs when a client redirects feelings from an earlier relationship, often a parent, onto the counsellor. Later psychodynamic thinkers, such as ego psychologists and object relations theorists, built on these ideas but stressed early relationships, the self and healthy development more than instinctual drives.

sections.heading: Freudian counselling
sections.text: Goals are insight and change: to make unconscious conflict conscious, work through transference, and strengthen the ego. Techniques include free association (saying whatever comes to mind), dream analysis, interpretation of resistance (the client avoiding painful material) and transference, and careful pacing. The counsellor listens for repeated patterns. Interpretation should be tentative and timed, not imposed.

sections.heading: Adlerian ideas
sections.text: Alfred Adler, once a colleague of Freud, saw people as goal-directed and socially embedded. Inferiority feelings are normal, especially in childhood; they can motivate striving for competence. A lifestyle is a person’s consistent pattern of beliefs, goals and behaviour. Social interest means feeling connected to others and wanting to contribute. Problems arise from discouragement, mistaken lifestyle convictions and low social interest. Adlerian goals are to encourage, correct mistaken beliefs and increase social interest. Techniques include lifestyle assessment (family constellation, early recollections), interpretation, encouragement and homework tasks.

sections.heading: Case and limits
sections.text: Case: Chidi, 22, avoids seminars. Psychodynamic formulation: criticism by his father left him fearing exposure; he represses anger and projects it onto lecturers, and treats the counsellor as a critical parent. Adlerian formulation: he feels inferior, aims to avoid failure, and shows low social interest. Both views suggest exploring early relationships and patterns; Adlerian work adds encouragement and small cooperative tasks. Evidence is uneven: short-term psychodynamic therapy has some research support, while Adlerian counselling has fewer controlled studies. Neither explains every problem.

keyPoints: The unconscious, defence mechanisms and transference are central Freudian ideas.
Later psychodynamic thinkers stress early relationships, the self and healthy development.
Freudian counselling aims at insight and works through transference and resistance.
Adlerians see inferiority feelings as normal and study a client’s lifestyle and social interest.
Adlerian counselling encourages clients and corrects mistaken beliefs.
Evidence is uneven, so use these approaches critically and integrate them with research and the client’s culture.

en.title: Person-Centred and Existential Counselling
en.short: Rogers’ core conditions and actualising tendency, existential themes, and a comparison of goals and roles.

sections.heading: Rogers and the actualising tendency
sections.text: Carl Rogers held that people have an actualising tendency: an innate drive to grow, maintain and fulfil their potential. Problems arise when conditions of worth, the conditional approval of others, distort the self-concept (how one sees oneself). Rogers proposed core conditions for therapeutic change. The best known are congruence (the counsellor is genuine), unconditional positive regard (warm acceptance without judgement) and empathic understanding (sensing the client’s world and communicating it). These create a safe climate in which the client can move towards a more fully functioning life.

sections.heading: Existential themes
sections.text: Existential counselling draws on philosophers such as Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger and Sartre, and on writers such as Viktor Frankl and Irvin Yalom. It examines universal concerns: death, freedom and responsibility, existential isolation (the gap between self and others), and meaninglessness. Yalom called these the four ultimate concerns. Freedom brings choice and responsibility, and with them existential anxiety, the unease that belongs to human existence. Neurotic anxiety is a defensive avoidance of that unease. The task is to face anxiety honestly and choose authentically.

sections.heading: Goals, techniques, role
sections.text: Person-centred goals are self-acceptance, congruence between self and experience, and becoming a fully functioning person. The counsellor works non-directively, using active listening and reflection of feeling rather than interpretation or advice. Existential goals are authentic living, acceptance of limits, and personally chosen meaning. Its methods include phenomenological exploration of the client’s experience (describing it as it appears, without judging it), dialogue, and gentle confrontation of avoidance; it is not a fixed technique package. The person-centred counsellor offers a relational climate. The existential counsellor joins the client in examining choices, mortality and responsibility, and may disclose their own presence as a fellow human.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Consider Ada, a Nigerian graduate who feels trapped by family expectations. A person-centred counsellor reflects her feelings and offers acceptance, helping her hear her own wants. An existential counsellor might ask what she would choose if no one judged her, and explore the anxiety of freedom. Both respect her autonomy; neither imposes a solution.

keyPoints: Rogers held that an actualising tendency drives growth, but conditions of worth can distort the self-concept.
The core conditions are congruence, unconditional positive regard and empathic understanding.
Existential counselling explores death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness, and the anxiety they raise.
Existential anxiety belongs to human existence; neurotic anxiety is a defensive avoidance of it.
Person-centred counselling is non-directive and relational; existential counselling is collaborative and explores choices.
Both approaches respect client autonomy and avoid imposing solutions.

en.title: Cognitive-Behavioural and Rational Emotive Counselling
en.short: Cognitive model, behavioural techniques, REBT ABC model, cognitive restructuring, homework and behavioural experiments.

sections.heading: Cognitive model
sections.text: Cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) rests on the cognitive model: events do not directly cause feelings and actions; our interpretations and beliefs do. A low mark can trigger 'I am stupid' and shame, or 'I need a better method' and determination. Automatic thoughts are quick, habitual interpretations; deeper beliefs lie behind them. The aim is accurate, balanced thinking, not forced positivity.

sections.heading: Behavioural methods
sections.text: Behavioural techniques change actions, because avoidance and inactivity maintain problems. Behavioural activation schedules necessary or rewarding activities. Graded tasks break a goal into small steps. Exposure means approaching a feared situation safely and repeatedly without escape, so fear reduces. Reinforcement, meaning rewarding a behaviour so it repeats, and skills training build new behaviour. These methods combine with cognitive work.

sections.heading: REBT and ABC
sections.text: Albert Ellis’s rational emotive behaviour therapy (REBT) uses the ABC model. A is the Activating event; B is the Belief about A; C is the emotional and behavioural Consequence. Irrational beliefs are rigid demands (must, should), awfulising ('this is terrible'), low frustration tolerance ('I cannot stand it') and global ratings ('I am worthless'). D is Disputation, examining evidence and logic. E is the Effective new belief. REBT is direct but respectful.

sections.heading: Restructuring and homework
sections.text: Cognitive restructuring means identifying a belief, testing its evidence and logic, and forming a balanced alternative. Homework carries this into daily life through thought records, activity logs and behavioural experiments. An experiment tests a prediction in reality. Example: Ada scores 48% on a practice test. A is the score; B is 'I must always pass, so I am worthless'; C is shame and avoidance. She disputes B: one score shows a study problem, not low human worth. Alternative: 'I prefer to pass, but I can learn from this.' Experiment: she predicts asking her lecturer for feedback will be humiliating, rating anxiety 80/100. She asks, gets specific feedback, and anxiety falls to 40/100. The result weakens the belief.

keyPoints: The cognitive model holds that interpretations and beliefs, not events alone, shape feelings and behaviour.
Behavioural techniques such as activation, graded tasks and exposure change avoidance and inactivity.
REBT’s ABC model links an Activating event, Beliefs and Consequences; D disputes irrational beliefs and E states an effective alternative.
Irrational beliefs include rigid musts, awfulising, low frustration tolerance and global self-ratings.
Cognitive restructuring tests a belief and builds a balanced alternative rather than repeating positive slogans.
Homework and behavioural experiments test predictions in real life and provide evidence for new beliefs.

en.title: Solution-Focused and Narrative Counselling
en.short: Solution-focused questions, narrative techniques, their postmodern roots and how they differ from problem-focused work.

sections.heading: Postmodern assumptions
sections.text: Both approaches rest on social constructionism: people make meaning through language and relationships, so there is no single objective truth about a life. The client, not the counsellor, is the expert on their own experience, and problems are patterns kept alive in talk rather than fixed defects inside a person. Solution-focused therapy was developed by Steve de Shazer and Insoo Kim Berg in Milwaukee, USA; narrative therapy by Michael White and David Epston in Australia and New Zealand.

sections.heading: Solution-focused questions
sections.text:
Instead of asking why a problem exists, the counsellor asks what the client wants instead. The miracle question: 'Suppose a miracle happened tonight and the problem was solved. How would you know tomorrow? What would be different, and who would notice first?' It builds a picture of the preferred future.

Scaling turns progress into a number: 'On a scale of 0 to 10, where 10 is the miracle, where are you today?' If the client says 3, ask what has already moved them from 0 to 3, and what a 4 would look like. Exceptions are times the problem could have appeared but did not. A student who says she always panics in exams may recall one test where she stayed calm; that exception is then studied.

sections.heading: Narrative ideas
sections.text: Externalising separates the person from the problem by naming it: 'the person is not the problem; the problem is the problem'. A counsellor asks a boy with a temper how 'the anger' gets him into trouble, and when he has resisted it. Unique outcomes, or sparkling moments, are small events that contradict the problem story. Re-authoring links them into a richer story in which the client is the agent.

sections.heading: Compared with problem-focused work
sections.text: Problem-focused approaches assess and analyse the problem before treating it. Solution-focused and narrative work spend little time on the problem’s history, holding that studying it can enlarge it. Critics say this may under-serve clients facing trauma or serious risk. Many counsellors borrow techniques from both.

keyPoints: Solution-focused therapy is a brief, postmodern approach; narrative therapy shares its postmodern base. Both treat the client as the expert.
The miracle question builds a detailed picture of the preferred future.
Scaling questions rate progress from 0 to 10 and identify small next steps.
Exceptions are times the problem did not occur; they reveal existing strengths.
Externalising separates the person from the problem, and unique outcomes and re-authoring build a new story.
Unlike problem-focused models, both spend little time analysing the problem’s history, which critics say may not suit trauma or high risk.

en.title: Career Guidance and Career Development
en.short: Career choice theories, career information, decision-making, employability, job search and life-stage counselling.

sections.heading: Theories of career choice
sections.text:
Trait-factor theory, linked to Frank Parsons, matches a person’s traits, such as interests, abilities and values, to the demands of an occupation. Holland’s RIASEC interest types (realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising and conventional) are often used this way. Developmental theory, especially Donald Super’s life-span, life-space model, sees careers as growing through stages: growth, exploration, establishment, maintenance and decline. It stresses career adaptability, the readiness to cope with changing work.

Social-cognitive career theory (Lent, Brown and Hackett) explains choice through self-efficacy (belief in one’s ability), outcome expectations (what one expects from an action), goals, and barriers or supports. Work adjustment theory (Dawis and Lofquist) focuses on correspondence between person and work environment: satisfaction (the worker is content) and satisfactoriness (the employer is content), with adjustment styles when the match breaks down.

sections.heading: Information and decisions
sections.text:
Career information must be accurate, current and local: education pathways, entry requirements, pay ranges, labour demand and working conditions. Check official sources because figures change by country and year. Good guidance challenges stereotypes and explains the hidden labour market, meaning jobs not advertised.

A structured decision model helps: define the decision, gather information, list options, weigh them against values and constraints, choose, make an action plan, and review. In a case, Amina, a final-year student in Kenya, wants accounting but fears maths. The counsellor explores her self-efficacy, arranges a bookkeeping course and a talk with an accountant, then reviews her confidence and choice.

sections.heading: Employability and job search
sections.text: Employability is the set of skills, qualifications, experience, networks and adaptability that help a person gain and keep work. Job search includes a clear CV, tailored applications, interview practice, professional networks and safe use of online profiles. Teach clients to check vacancies for scams and to record applications.

sections.heading: Clients across life stages
sections.text: Counselling changes with life stage. School leavers need subject and pathway information; graduates need job-search skills and realistic expectations; mid-career adults may face redundancy or retraining; older workers may plan retirement or gradual withdrawal from work. Unemployment, disability, migration and family roles affect decisions. Use the same exploration, but respect each client’s context and autonomy.

keyPoints: Trait-factor theory matches personal traits to occupational demands; Holland’s RIASEC types are one example.
Super’s developmental theory describes career stages and career adaptability across the life span.
Social-cognitive career theory links self-efficacy, outcome expectations, goals and barriers or supports.
Work adjustment theory measures person-environment correspondence through satisfaction and satisfactoriness.
Career information must be accurate, current and local, and decision-making should be structured and reviewed.
Employability and job search skills include networks, tailored applications and safe online use, with counselling adapted to life stage.

en.title: Educational Guidance and School Counselling
en.short: School guidance services: orientation, study skills, course choice, exam anxiety, attendance and referral.

sections.heading: What educational guidance covers
sections.text: Educational guidance helps students make informed choices about learning and progress. It is not the same as personal counselling, though the two overlap. School counselling is a planned service that supports academic, personal and social development. In schools and colleges it usually includes orientation, study skills, subject and course choice, examination anxiety, attendance and referral. Arrangements differ by country and institution, so students should check local policy.

sections.heading: Services in practice
sections.text: Orientation introduces new students to rules, facilities, staff and support services. Study-skills guidance teaches time management, note making, reading for meaning and revision. Subject and course choice guidance matches interests and results to requirements, without taking the decision from the student. For examination anxiety, the counsellor can teach breathing, planning and realistic self-talk, and refer severe cases. Attendance work looks for causes such as illness, bullying, family pressure or disengagement. Referral means passing a case, with consent where possible, to a suitable professional or agency.

sections.heading: The counsellor in school
sections.text: The counsellor coordinates guidance, keeps records, runs group sessions and sees students individually. The role is helping, not disciplining. Confidentiality has limits: risk of harm, abuse or legal duty may require disclosure. The counsellor also advises the school on policies that affect student welfare.

sections.heading: Working with others
sections.text: Teachers notice changes in attendance or work and can refer. Parents give information and support plans. Example: Amina, in a Lagos college, misses classes and fears mathematics. The counsellor talks with her, checks her timetable, teaches a study plan, and with consent meets her teacher and mother. They agree on extra practice and a review date. If panic continues, the counsellor refers her to a clinic.

keyPoints: Educational guidance helps students with learning choices, while school counselling supports academic, personal and social development.
Orientation, study skills, subject choice, examination anxiety, attendance and referral are core school guidance services.
Referral means passing a case to a suitable professional or agency, with consent where possible.
The counsellor coordinates support and does not act as a disciplinarian; confidentiality has legal and safety limits.
Teachers and parents are partners: they notice problems, give information and help carry out plans.
Severe examination anxiety or persistent absence should be referred rather than kept within routine guidance.

en.title: Personal and Social Counselling
en.short: Counselling self-esteem, relationships, anger, stress, identity, adjustment, risk assessment and referral.

sections.heading: Structured helping model
sections.text: A simple structured model has five stages: connect, assess, agree goals, act and review. Connect means building trust and explaining confidentiality (privacy) and its limits. Assess means exploring the concern, history, strengths, supports and risk. Agree goals means choosing small, concrete changes. Act means psychoeducation (teaching about the problem), problem-solving and practice tasks. Review means checking progress and planning ending or referral.

sections.heading: Common concerns
sections.text: Self-esteem is a person’s overall judgement of worth; low self-esteem often follows harsh self-talk, so help clients notice evidence and set achievable tasks. Relationship work explores communication, boundaries (limits a person sets), expectations and conflict patterns. Anger is normal; help clients notice early body signs, pause and choose safe expression. Stress is strain when demands exceed perceived resources; teach breathing, planning and rest. Identity is the sense of who one is, including culture, values and roles; explore rather than advise. Adjustment is coping with change such as school, work or migration; normalise it and build routines.

sections.heading: Risk and referral
sections.text: Assess risk at first contact and when information changes. Ask directly about self-harm, suicide, harm to others and abuse. If risk is imminent, do not leave the person alone; follow local emergency and safeguarding (protecting people from harm) procedures and contact a supervisor. Refer when concerns exceed your training, symptoms are severe or persistent, or specialised care is needed. Referral means handing over care with consent where possible, giving clear reasons and contact details. Keep within competence and use supervision.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Amina, a second-year student, says she is worthless and has stopped attending classes after a breakup. The counsellor listens, assesses mood, sleep, support and risk. Amina denies suicidal thoughts. They agree two goals: attend one class daily and contact a friend weekly. The counsellor teaches a thought-checking task and reviews after two weeks. When her symptoms persist, the counsellor refers her to the campus health service and continues supportive contact.

keyPoints: Use a five-stage model: connect, assess, agree goals, act and review.
Explore self-esteem, relationships, anger, stress, identity and adjustment as normal life concerns.
Ask directly about self-harm, suicide, harm to others and abuse.
Imminent risk requires immediate safety action and local emergency or safeguarding procedures.
Refer when needs exceed your competence, symptoms are severe or persistent, or specialised care is needed.
Supervision supports safe practice and clear referral.

en.title: Group Counselling: Process, Ethics and Practice
en.short: Group types, stages, dynamics, leadership, screening, ethics, a short group plan and conflict handling.

sections.heading: Types and screening
sections.text: Common group types include psychoeducational groups, which teach a skill; counselling groups, which use interaction to help personal concerns; support groups, which share a life experience; and task groups, which work on a job. Therapy groups treat deeper clinical issues and need specialist training. Screening is an individual interview before joining. It checks goals, readiness, risk, fit and informed consent, and allows referral if a group is unsuitable.

sections.heading: Stages and dynamics
sections.text: Group development usually moves through forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. Forming is polite orientation; storming brings disagreement about roles and power; norming sets norms, the shared rules of behaviour; performing is productive work; adjourning is ending and review. Group dynamics are the forces between members: roles, norms, cohesion (attraction and trust), communication patterns, power and resistance. A counsellor observes these and uses them in the here-and-now.

sections.heading: Leadership and ethics
sections.text: Leadership skills include structuring sessions, linking members, modelling respect, blocking harmful behaviour, drawing out quiet members and managing time. Informed consent explains purpose, procedures, risks and the limits of confidentiality. Group confidentiality cannot be guaranteed because members may disclose outside; the leader asks for a written or verbal agreement and states legal and safety exceptions. Ethical issues include competence, dual relationships, boundaries, cultural sensitivity and referral.

sections.heading: Short group plan and conflict
sections.text: Plan: a closed counselling group (no new members) of eight members, six weekly 90-minute sessions, after screening. Session one sets goals and ground rules; two to five use structured activities and discussion; six reviews and ends. Evaluate with a brief member rating. If conflict arises, for example Amina and Chidi argue over advice, the leader names the tension, stays neutral, reminds members of ground rules, asks for I-statements (speaking from one’s own experience) and focuses on the process. Check safety; refer if threats or distress exceed the group’s scope.

keyPoints: Group types include psychoeducational, counselling, support and task groups.
Screening is an individual pre-group interview for goals, readiness, risk and fit.
Groups commonly move through forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning.
Group dynamics include roles, norms, cohesion, power and communication.
Leaders structure, link, model, block harmful behaviour and manage confidentiality limits.
In conflict, name it, stay neutral, use ground rules and I-statements, and check safety.

en.title: Family and Couple Counselling
en.short: Family systems, communication, boundaries, genograms, couple and family skills, and referral.

sections.heading: Family as a system
sections.text: Family systems theory views the family as a connected system: each member affects the others, and problems are understood in relationships, not only inside one person. It speaks of circular causality, where actions and reactions loop, and homeostasis, the pull to keep familiar patterns even when they cause pain. Subsystems are smaller units such as parents or siblings. Roles are the expected parts people play, for example the peacemaker or the responsible eldest child. These ideas help the counsellor avoid blaming one member.

sections.heading: Patterns and boundaries
sections.text: Communication patterns include who speaks, who is heard and how conflict is handled. A common pattern is pursuer and withdrawer: one partner seeks contact while the other retreats. Boundaries are the rules about closeness and distance between members and outsiders. Clear boundaries allow support and independence; very rigid or very diffuse boundaries can cause distress. Couple work often starts by naming these patterns without taking sides.

sections.heading: Assessment and genogram
sections.text: Assessment explores the presenting problem, its history, family structure, roles, rules, communication, strengths, culture, health and safety. A genogram is a family map, usually with squares for males, circles for females, a line for a couple and branches for children; it records names, ages, illnesses and close relationships. It can reveal repeated patterns. In one case, a couple argued about money. The genogram showed both had grown up with secret debts and sudden crises. Naming this pattern reduced blame and opened a calmer conversation.

sections.heading: Skills and referral
sections.text: Basic skills include joining, active listening, circular questioning, reframing and communication exercises. Ask each person what they notice and what they would prefer. Agree small homework tasks, such as a ten-minute daily talk without phones. Work with consent, confidentiality and its limits. Refer for specialist therapy when there is domestic violence, child abuse, suicidal risk, severe mental illness, addiction, or legal or custody disputes. In those cases, safety planning and outside services come before relationship work.

keyPoints: Family systems theory sees problems in relationships, not only in one person.
Circular causality and homeostasis explain repeating family patterns.
Roles and boundaries shape closeness, conflict and support.
A genogram maps family structure and repeated patterns across generations.
Basic skills include joining, circular questioning, reframing and communication tasks.
Refer when there is violence, abuse, suicidal risk, severe mental illness, addiction or legal dispute.

en.title: Counselling Children and Adolescents
en.short: Developmental fit, play methods, consent and confidentiality with minors, work with parents and schools, and common concerns.

sections.heading: Developmental fit
sections.text:
Children’s counselling adapts to age. A seven-year-old may think in concrete terms and explain feelings through play; an adolescent can reflect abstractly but may value privacy and peer approval. Use short sentences, familiar words and check understanding. Assess attention span, language and family culture. Do not treat a child as a small adult.

The counsellor also considers attachment, schooling and any developmental delay, and chooses goals the child can understand.

sections.heading: Play and activity
sections.text:
Play and activity methods give children a safe way to express what they cannot say. Non-directive play therapy lets the child lead; art, puppets, sand tray, stories, games and role play can open themes.

The counsellor observes, reflects feeling and sets clear limits, such as no hurting. Activities must suit age and culture. They support counselling but do not replace assessment or protection when there is risk.

sections.heading: Consent and confidentiality
sections.text:
Consent for a minor is governed by national law and local policy, which vary; check the current rule. Usually a parent or guardian consents and the child gives assent, meaning the child agrees after the process is explained in simple words.

Explain confidentiality and its limits at the start: safety concerns, abuse or serious harm may require sharing with parents, school or authorities. Share only what is necessary. Record decisions. A mature adolescent may have stronger rights in some countries, but do not assume.

sections.heading: Parents, schools, concerns
sections.text:
Work with parents and school staff as partners, with agreed boundaries. Ask what each needs to know and get consent where possible. For bullying, assess repetition, power imbalance and safety, then plan with the school. For bereavement, match explanations to the child’s understanding of death and allow grief. For behaviour difficulties, use functional assessment: what happens before, the behaviour, and the consequence.

Case: Amina, 9, is hit at school. The counsellor checks safety, involves her mother and teacher, and uses puppet play to rehearse asking for help.

keyPoints: Adapt methods to the child’s developmental stage, language and culture.
Play and activity methods let children express feelings, with clear limits.
Consent rules for minors vary by country; usually a parent or guardian consents and the child gives assent.
Explain confidentiality limits at the start and share only necessary information.
Work with parents and schools with agreed boundaries and consent.
For bullying assess safety and power imbalance; for bereavement match explanations to understanding; for behaviour difficulties use functional assessment.

en.title: Assessment and Psychometrics in Counselling
en.short: Choosing, giving, scoring and interpreting tests, plus interviews, observation, rating scales and cultural fairness.

sections.heading: Selecting and giving tests
sections.text:
Assessment is the systematic gathering of information about a person. Psychometrics is the science of measuring psychological qualities and judging how well a test does so. Select a test by its purpose, the client’s age and language, the evidence for its scores, and your training. Read the manual.

Administration follows standard instructions, time limits and materials, with consent and confidentiality. Check scoring. A raw score is the number of correct answers or points. It is often converted to a standard score. If a client scores 42, the norm mean is 50 and the standard deviation is 10, then z = (42 − 50) ÷ 10 = −0.8, below the mean. Interpret cautiously, with the client, and never from one test alone.

sections.heading: Reliability and validity
sections.text: Reliability is consistency of scores. Test-retest reliability checks stability over time; internal consistency checks whether items measure one construct; inter-rater reliability checks agreement between scorers. Validity is whether a test measures what it claims and supports the decisions made. Content validity covers the domain; construct validity covers the underlying trait; criterion validity compares scores with an outside standard. A reliable test can still be invalid.

sections.heading: Norms and fairness
sections.text: Norms are the scores of a reference group used to compare a client. Check whether the norm group matches the client in age, education, language and culture, and whether the norms are current. Fairness means giving all clients a fair chance to show ability. Cultural bias occurs when items, language or expectations favour one group. Use local norms where they exist, adapt tests properly, and treat differences as information, not deficiency.

sections.heading: Other methods and limits
sections.text: Interviews range from unstructured to structured. Structured interviews use set questions and scoring, which improves consistency. Observation records behaviour in natural or controlled settings; note context and observer bias. Rating scales, such as Likert scales, turn judgements into numbers, but halo effects (one impression colouring all ratings) and social desirability (answering to look good) distort them. Tests sample behaviour and carry error. They can label people, and they cannot replace clinical judgement. Use multiple methods, explain limits, and keep records secure.

keyPoints: Select tests by purpose, client characteristics, evidence and your training.
Standard administration, consent and checked scoring protect the meaning of scores.
A z-score is z = (X − mean) ÷ standard deviation; for X = 42, mean = 50 and SD = 10, z = −0.8.
Reliability is consistency; validity is whether a test measures what it claims and supports decisions.
Norms must match the client and be current; cultural bias can make scores unfair.
Interviews, observation and rating scales add information, but tests are samples and cannot replace judgement.

en.title: Crisis Intervention and Grief Counselling
en.short: Crisis assessment, safety planning, psychological first aid, referral, and grief models after loss.

sections.heading: Crisis and assessment
sections.text: A crisis is an event or appraisal that overwhelms a person’s usual coping. Assess immediate danger: risk of harm to self or others, medical needs, disorientation, access to means, substance use, supports and previous attempts. Ask directly about suicide; asking does not plant the idea. If danger is immediate, do not leave the person alone. Involve emergency services and a trusted person, and explain the limits of confidentiality.

sections.heading: Safety and first aid
sections.text: Safety planning is a written, collaborative list of warning signs, coping steps, people and places that help, means restriction (limiting access to harmful methods), and emergency and professional contacts. Psychological first aid (PFA) is a humane, supportive response, not therapy. It offers safety and comfort, stabilisation, practical help, information, and connection to supports and services. Do not force a recounting of the event. For example, Amina, a 19-year-old student, survives a flood that killed her sister. She is safe but sleepless and guilty. The counsellor gives PFA, helps her contact family, makes a safety plan, refers her for a medical check, and books follow-up.

sections.heading: Grief and loss
sections.text: Grief is the response to loss; mourning is its cultural expression. Kübler-Ross described five stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. They are not linear or universal. Worden’s tasks are to accept the reality of loss, process the pain, adjust to life without the person, and relocate the bond. The dual process model describes oscillation between loss-oriented and restoration-oriented coping. Continuing bonds means maintaining a changed relationship with the deceased. After death, disaster, violence or separation, allow cultural rituals and do not pathologise normal grief.

sections.heading: Referral and follow-up
sections.text: Referral means linking the person to another service, such as medical, psychiatric, safeguarding or specialist bereavement care. Know your limits and obtain consent where possible. Follow-up means planned contact to review risk, check whether referral happened, and address barriers. Record actions and coordinate care. Prolonged grief disorder is a specialist diagnosis with criteria and time limits; do not apply it casually.

keyPoints: Crisis assessment checks immediate danger, medical needs, supports and suicide risk, and asking directly is safe.
If danger is immediate, do not leave the person alone; involve emergency services and a trusted person.
Safety planning lists warning signs, coping steps, supports, means restriction and emergency contacts.
Psychological first aid offers safety, comfort, practical help and connection, not forced recounting.
Grief models such as Kübler-Ross, Worden’s tasks and the dual process model guide, not prescribe, care.
Refer and follow up: know limits, obtain consent where possible, record actions and review risk.

en.title: Substance Use and Addiction Counselling
en.short: Covers models, screening, stages of change, motivational interviewing, relapse prevention and referral.

sections.heading: Models and language
sections.text:
Addiction is best understood through a biopsychosocial model: biological factors such as genetics, psychological factors such as learning and coping, and social factors such as family, peers, poverty and availability. The disease model treats addiction as a chronic condition; learning models stress cues and rewards. These views can be combined.

Use person-first language: say 'a person with a substance use disorder', not 'an addict'. This reduces stigma, which can stop people seeking help.

sections.heading: Screening and assessment
sections.text:
Screening uses short validated tools to find possible problems. The WHO’s AUDIT (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test) screens alcohol use; other tools cover drugs. A positive screen is not a diagnosis.

Assessment explores the substance, amount, frequency, duration, consequences, withdrawal risk, physical and mental health, and social supports. Ask about suicide risk and previous treatment. Consent and confidentiality apply, within legal and ethical limits. If withdrawal could be dangerous, refer for medical review before counselling alone.

sections.heading: Change and counselling
sections.text:
The Stages of Change model describes precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance. People move back and forth between stages, and relapse means returning to an earlier one. Motivational interviewing is a collaborative, goal-oriented style that strengthens a person’s own reasons for change and respects autonomy. Counsellors use open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries.

A small case: Amina, a student in Kano, is unsure about stopping cannabis. Her counsellor reflects her mixed feelings, explores her values, and offers information only with permission. She agrees to a small step: recording her use for two weeks.

sections.heading: Relapse and referral
sections.text:
Relapse prevention helps the person identify high-risk situations, triggers, early warning signs and coping plans. A lapse is a single return to use; a relapse is a return to a pattern. Treat both as learning points, not failure.

Referral means linking the person to medical, mental health, family or social services with consent. Laws differ by country: some use criminal penalties, others health-based approaches. Culture shapes family roles, meaning and stigma. Know local law and services, and check current rules.

keyPoints: Addiction is best explained by a biopsychosocial model that combines biological, psychological and social factors.
Screening tools such as the WHO AUDIT suggest risk but do not diagnose; assessment explores pattern, consequences, withdrawal and mental health.
The Stages of Change model describes precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance; relapse means returning to an earlier stage.
Motivational interviewing is collaborative and autonomy-supporting, and it draws out the person’s own reasons for change.
Relapse prevention identifies high-risk situations and coping plans; a lapse is not a failure.
Refer with consent and follow local law, which differs by country, while using person-first, non-stigmatising language.

en.title: Multicultural and Diversity Counselling
en.short: Culture, ethnicity, religion, gender, disability, class, sexuality, competence, bias and interpreters.

sections.heading: Culture and identity
sections.text: Culture is the learned and shared beliefs, values, language and customs of a group; it is not fixed, and people vary within it. Ethnicity concerns a person’s sense of belonging to a group with shared ancestry or history. Religion and spirituality give meaning, rules and coping resources. Gender is social expectation attached to sex, while sexuality concerns attraction and identity. Disability is both an impairment and a barrier created by society. Class means socioeconomic position, shaped by income, education and status. Intersectionality means these identities interact; a disabled woman from a poor family may face combined disadvantage.

sections.heading: Competence, power and bias
sections.text: Cultural competence is often taught as awareness of one’s own culture, knowledge of clients’ cultures, and skills for working across difference. Cultural humility adds lifelong openness, self-critique and repair of power imbalance. The counsellor holds power through expertise, diagnosis, records and fees. Bias may be explicit or implicit, and it can affect listening, assessment and referral. Reflect on assumptions, seek supervision, and check how racism, sexism, ableism and class prejudice may operate in the room and in the institution.

sections.heading: Interpreters and adaptation
sections.text: Use a trained interpreter when language difference is substantial, not a child or a family member. Brief the interpreter on confidentiality and roles, speak to the client not the interpreter, and check understanding. Adapt approaches by asking what the problem means to this person, using their language and metaphors, and negotiating goals. Treat cultural patterns as questions, not conclusions. In a case, a counsellor in Nairobi meets Amina, a Somali refugee. He avoids assuming family collectivism; he asks who should be involved, offers a female interpreter, and checks religious and safety concerns.

keyPoints: Culture is learned, shared and changing, and clients vary within any cultural group.
Cultural competence combines awareness, knowledge and skills, while cultural humility adds ongoing self-critique and attention to power.
Counsellor power and bias can affect listening, assessment and referral, so use supervision and client feedback.
Use a trained interpreter, speak directly to the client and check that meaning is shared.
Adapt counselling to the client’s own explanation and goals, and treat group patterns as hypotheses rather than facts.
Ask about religion, gender, disability, class and sexuality, and consider how identities intersect.

en.title: Professional Practice, Law and Ethics
en.short: Codes, registration, negligence, confidentiality, records, child protection, duty to warn and court work.

sections.heading: Codes and registration
sections.text: Professional codes set standards for competence, consent, confidentiality, boundaries, supervision and continuing development. Registration and training vary by country. Some countries license counsellors by statute; others rely on voluntary registers or professional associations. In Nigeria, the Counselling Association of Nigeria (CASSON) is a professional body; statutory licensing is not universal. In the United Kingdom, counselling and psychotherapy are not statutorily regulated, and practitioners may join a voluntary register. Check your national regulator, qualification route and protected titles.

sections.heading: Legal duties and negligence
