sections.text: Legal duties include a duty of care, competence, informed consent, confidentiality and safe record keeping. Negligence has four elements: a duty of care, a breach of that duty, causation, and harm. In a hypothetical case, a counsellor in Lagos, Nigeria, sees a client who reports suicidal thoughts. If the counsellor ignores the risk and gives no referral, a negligence claim could ask whether a reasonable counsellor would have assessed and referred. The standard comes from national law and professional codes, so check current law.

sections.heading: Confidentiality and records
sections.text: Confidentiality is not absolute. Limits include client consent, serious risk to self or others, child protection, court order, supervision and agency policy. A duty to warn or protect a third party exists in some jurisdictions, for example in some US states after the Tarasoff court case (1976). It is not universal. Where national law imposes it, follow the law; otherwise do not assume it. Records should be accurate, factual, secure and kept only as long as national law requires. Clients may have a legal right to access their records.

sections.heading: Child protection and court
sections.text: Child protection laws vary. Many countries require counsellors to report suspected abuse to a child protection authority. Amina, 15, tells her counsellor that her uncle is abusing her. The counsellor explains the limits of confidentiality, records the facts, and reports if national law requires. She does not investigate. In court work, a counsellor may receive a subpoena or court order. A subpoena is a court order to attend court or to produce records. Seek legal advice, release only what is required, and distinguish fact from opinion.

keyPoints: Professional codes set standards, but registration and training requirements vary by country; check your national regulator.
Negligence requires duty of care, breach, causation and harm.
Confidentiality has legal limits, including serious risk, child protection and court orders.
A duty to warn or protect third parties exists only where national law imposes it; Tarasoff (1976) is a US example, not a universal rule.
Child protection laws may require reporting suspected abuse to an authority; counsellors should not investigate.
In court work, release only what is legally required and distinguish fact from opinion.

en.title: Practicum and Case Management
en.short: Contracting, records, case notes, formulation, referral, teamwork, supervision, conduct, case presentation and reflective log.

sections.heading: Starting the practicum
sections.text:
A practicum is supervised practical training in a real or simulated counselling setting. It begins with a contract: a written agreement between trainee, placement and supervisor. It states goals, roles, hours, confidentiality and its limits, record keeping, referral routes, supervision times and how progress is reviewed. Requirements differ by country and professional body, so check your programme and local counselling association.

Professional conduct means acting within your competence, keeping boundaries, protecting confidentiality, being fair, and seeking help early when unsure.

sections.heading: Records and formulation
sections.text:
Record keeping means creating and storing client information securely and lawfully. Write case notes soon after sessions, keep them factual and brief, distinguish observation from inference, and follow local policy on access, storage and retention. Many services use a structured note such as SOAP: subjective, objective, assessment, plan; formats vary.

Case formulation is a reasoned explanation of the client’s difficulties. It links presenting problems to predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors, and guides goals and interventions. A formulation is a working hypothesis, not a label.

sections.heading: Referral and teamwork
sections.text:
Case management is the planned coordination of a client’s care across services: assess needs, plan, refer, monitor and review. Referral means directing a client to another service when needs exceed your competence or role, when risk is urgent, or when specialist help is needed. Obtain consent where possible, explain why, and send only necessary information. Multidisciplinary work means cooperating with doctors, teachers, social workers and others while keeping role boundaries clear.

Supervision is regular, structured discussion with a qualified supervisor. Use it for stuck points, ethical doubts and skill development; it is not personal therapy. Bring concise notes and clear questions.

sections.heading: Presenting and reflecting
sections.text:
A case presentation usually covers anonymised background, presenting concern, relevant history and risk, formulation, work done, supervision question and plan. Example: a 19-year-old student misses classes after bereavement; the trainee notes sleep loss, no self-harm, and agrees a referral for grief support.

A reflective log records what happened, your thoughts and feelings, what you learned, what you would do differently, links to theory and ethics, and questions for supervision. Write it regularly and remove identifying details.

keyPoints: A practicum contract sets out goals, roles, confidentiality limits, records, referral and supervision.
Case notes should be timely, factual, secure and kept under local policy.
Case formulation is a working hypothesis linking problems to predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors.
Refer when needs exceed competence or risk is urgent, with consent where possible.
Supervision supports practice and is not personal therapy.
A reflective log and structured case presentation turn experience into learning.

en.title: Research Methods and Programme Evaluation
en.short: Quantitative and qualitative designs, sampling, ethics, analysis, needs assessment and small project reporting.

sections.heading: Designs and sampling
sections.text: Quantitative designs collect numbers. Common ones are surveys, pre-post studies (before and after measures) and quasi-experiments, which compare groups without random assignment. Qualitative designs collect words and meanings, using interviews, focus groups, observation or case studies. Mixed methods combine both. Sampling is choosing participants. Random sampling gives everyone a known chance; purposive sampling selects people for a reason; convenience sampling uses whoever is available. Report how you sampled and any bias (slant that distorts results).

sections.heading: Data and ethics
sections.text: Questionnaires are cheap but need clear items and a pilot test, a small trial run. Interviews give depth but need consent to record. Observation must respect privacy. Ethics require informed consent (voluntary agreement after full information), confidentiality, anonymity where possible, and no harm. Seek approval from your institution or counselling service. Store data securely. In a small project, keep the sample modest and say what you cannot generalise.

sections.heading: Analysis and reporting
sections.text: Basic quantitative analysis uses frequencies, percentages and means. For example, if 45 of 60 students want career guidance, the percentage is 45 ÷ 60 × 100 = 75%. The mean of scores 40, 50, 60, 70 and 80 is 300 ÷ 5 = 60. Qualitative analysis groups repeated ideas into themes. Report the aim, method, sample, instruments (questionnaires or interview guides), ethics, results and limitations. Link findings to counselling practice and avoid claiming more than the data show.

sections.heading: Needs and evaluation
sections.text: A needs assessment asks what a group needs before planning. A programme evaluation judges whether a service was delivered as planned (process) and whether it helped (outcome). Use clear questions and simple indicators (signs you can measure). A small counselling project can follow this order: define the question, read a few sources, choose a design and sample, prepare instruments, obtain ethics approval, collect and analyse data, then write a short report with recommendations.

keyPoints: Quantitative designs use numbers; qualitative designs explore meanings; mixed methods combine both.
Random sampling gives everyone a known chance; purposive sampling selects for a reason; convenience sampling uses available people and risks bias.
Ethics require informed consent, confidentiality, no harm and approval.
Percentage = (part ÷ whole) × 100; mean = sum of scores ÷ number of scores.
Needs assessment identifies gaps before planning; programme evaluation checks process and outcome.
A small project reports aim, method, sample, instruments, ethics, results, limitations and recommendations.

en.title: Advanced Counselling Theory and Integration
en.short: Compare major orientations, common factors, formulation and evidence for integrative practice.

sections.heading: Comparing orientations
sections.text:
Compare theories on their view of human nature, the source of distress, the mechanism of change, the therapist’s role and their evidence. Psychodynamic work assumes unconscious conflict and developmental history; cognitive-behavioural work assumes learned and cognitive mediation; person-centred work trusts the actualising tendency and the relationship; systemic work explains problems through circular patterns in relationships.

Each is a lens, not a complete truth. A critique asks what the theory explains well, what it ignores, and whether its claims can be tested.

sections.heading: Routes to integration
sections.text:
Theoretical integration combines concepts into a new model. Assimilative integration keeps one main orientation but borrows techniques. Technical eclecticism selects methods by evidence or fit without a unifying theory.

The common factors approach emphasises ingredients shared by effective therapies, especially the alliance, empathy, agreed goals and positive expectations. Integration must be coherent and accountable, not a random mixture.

sections.heading: Formulation and case
sections.text:
Formulation is an individual, hypothesis-based explanation of why this person has this problem now. It commonly links predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors.

Consider Amina, 29, in Lagos, who develops panic attacks after a job loss. Formulation might link earlier anxiety, the redundancy, avoidance and her supportive church group. Integrative practice could combine CBT breathing and graded exposure with a person-centred alliance, then review outcomes.

sections.heading: Evidence and limits
sections.text:
Evidence-based practice combines research, therapist expertise and client preferences. Trials and meta-analyses generally support several orientations for common problems; CBT has a strong evidence base for many anxiety and depressive disorders, while other approaches also have support.

Differences between bona fide therapies are often modest, and common factors matter, but this does not make techniques irrelevant. Evidence varies by problem, culture and setting, so monitor progress and adapt.

keyPoints: Theories differ in assumptions about human nature, distress and change, so comparison should examine those assumptions.
Integration has several forms: theoretical integration, assimilative integration, technical eclecticism and common factors.
Formulation is an idiographic hypothesis linking predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors.
Common factors include alliance, empathy, goals and expectations, but they do not replace tested techniques.
Evidence-based practice combines research, expertise and client preference and varies by problem and culture.
Monitor outcomes and revise the formulation rather than forcing the client into one theory.

en.title: Advanced Research Methods and Dissertation
en.short: Designs, systematic reviews, qualitative analysis, instruments, ethics, data and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: Designing the study
sections.text: Advanced design starts with the question, not the method. A design is defensible when the question, the evidence you will collect and the analysis fit together. Counselling research often uses mixed methods, which combine numbers and words. State your sampling plan and how you will judge quality. For quantitative work this means validity (does the instrument measure what it claims) and reliability (does it give consistent results). For qualitative work it means trustworthiness: credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability.

sections.heading: Systematic review
sections.text: A systematic review answers a focused question by finding, appraising and combining all relevant studies. Register a protocol first, for example with PROSPERO, an international register for reviews in health and social care. Search at least two databases, record your search strings and dates, and state inclusion and exclusion criteria. Screen in duplicate where possible. Report the flow of studies and assess risk of bias. A meta-analysis pools results statistically; use it only when studies are similar enough.

sections.heading: Qualitative analysis and instruments
sections.text: Thematic analysis groups coded text into themes. Read transcripts, code openly, compare codes, then define themes and keep an audit trail. A theme is an interpretation, not a frequency count. Instrument development follows steps: define the construct, write items, get expert review, pilot, then test. Example: a 20-item scale piloted on 60 students, with 4 items removed, leaves 16 items; the retention rate is 16 ÷ 20 = 80%. Report reliability, such as Cronbach’s alpha, and validity evidence.

sections.heading: Ethics, data and writing
sections.text: Seek ethics approval before collecting data. In Nigeria this is usually a university or hospital research ethics committee; rules differ by country, so check your institution’s current requirements. Cover informed consent, confidentiality and a plan for distressed participants. Store data securely, anonymise it early, and keep it for the period your policy states. Write the dissertation as argument, not diary: introduction, literature review, methods, results, discussion, limitations, references. Defend by knowing your choices.

keyPoints: The research question, evidence and analysis must fit together.
Mixed methods combine quantitative and qualitative data.
Quantitative quality means validity and reliability; qualitative quality means trustworthiness.
Register a systematic review protocol and record searches and criteria.
Instrument development runs from construct definition to pilot testing and reliability checks.
Get ethics approval before data collection and keep data secure and anonymised.

en.title: Advanced Supervision and Training
en.short: Supervision models, contracts, feedback, evaluation, ethics, culture and CPD for counsellors.

sections.heading: Models and functions
sections.text: Supervision is a structured relationship in which a more experienced practitioner helps a counsellor reflect, learn and keep standards. Common models include developmental models, which adjust support to the supervisee’s experience, process models, which focus on the supervision session itself, and integrative models. A widely used framework is Proctor’s three functions: normative (quality and standards), formative (learning and reflection) and restorative (support). Kadushin’s administrative, educational and supportive functions overlap with these. Supervision is not therapy, though it can be supportive.

sections.heading: Contract and relationship
sections.text: A supervision contract is an agreement, usually written, covering purpose, roles, frequency, confidentiality and its limits, records, evaluation, fees if any, and a review date. It protects both parties and gives informed consent. The supervisory relationship needs trust, honesty and attention to power. The supervisor assesses, so the supervisee may hide mistakes. Agreed boundaries, regular review and a non-punitive stance help. Case: Amina, a counsellor in Kano, agrees with her supervisor to bring one difficult case each month and to say when she feels stuck.

sections.heading: Feedback and evaluation
sections.text: Feedback should be timely, specific, behavioural and owned by the giver. Ask permission, describe what you observed, and check understanding. In a triad role-play, one student counsels, one supervises and one observes; the observer gives one strength and one change, using an example. Evaluation is formative (ongoing) and summative (end-point). Use agreed criteria and separate evaluation from support. Record evidence and give the supervisee a chance to respond.

sections.heading: Ethics, culture and CPD
sections.text: Supervisors need competence, confidentiality, clear boundaries and informed consent. They avoid dual relationships and manage conflicts of interest. Cultural humility matters: discuss culture, language, religion and power openly, and avoid treating one cultural norm as universal. Training for supervision includes formal study, supervised practice and feedback on recorded or observed work. Continuing professional development (CPD) can include workshops, reading, peer supervision and reflective logs. Keep records and review competence regularly.

keyPoints: Supervision has normative, formative and restorative functions.
A supervision contract sets purpose, roles, confidentiality, records, evaluation and review.
Feedback should be timely, specific, behavioural and checked with the supervisee.
Evaluation uses agreed criteria and separates formative from summative judgements.
Ethical supervision covers competence, boundaries, consent and cultural humility.
Supervisor training and CPD continue through supervised practice, feedback and reflection.
